title: Knowing your lick ahead of time and fitting the band
summary: Ridgley says a player must know the lick before starting it, and that the band expects something fitting in the gap. Banjo, bass and piano go along while others rest.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Lips, teeth and breath: the physical craft of brass playing

blocks.x: When, let's say we're just starting off and you're playing this background music now, old Maryland, my Maryland. As soon as you start playing, do you call it a riff or a…
A lick he said. A lick.
Is that what you would call it? Bum bum, a bum bum bum bum bum bum. Would you call that a lick or what?
Well, I'll tell you, I wouldn't know what to call it, unless you just put it in there. I see.

Well, let's call it a lick so we'll have something to talk about. Yeah. Before you start that lick, do you know what you're going to do ahead of time? Is your mind told you ahead what you're going to do? Yeah, yeah, yeah.
You know you're going to do that.
I see. You never start playing a lick before you know what lick you're going to complete. That's right. So you know where you're going before you start.

Boy, that's the best way always, you see. To know that's the same as going up the ladder down, you know, where you're going to stop when you go, you know where you're going to stop when you come down. Now you just go into, like you said, putting that lick as you call it like that. You have to know that in the band, you have to know it too. And then they expect that out of you.

They expect that from you. Yeah. Well, now if they expect that from you, and you're, say you've got, you're going to play six choruses at Maryland, then don't you do the same thing on the other five choruses when you don't have the melody? Or do you take different licks but in the same hole, so to speak? So they expect a lick from you in a hole, but they don't know exactly what lick you're going to play.

They expect, as you said, they expect it, but they don't know. But you know that you're going to make something that's going to accord with them, don't you know? They're not going to throw you. At least make something that don't sound good in that spot.
That'll sound good in that spot with the melody line.

Yeah. You're worrying about it. You carry that melody, that little solo, as we would call it, or Maryland. Then you take that vamp and you use something like that. Now, you know the rest of your band, they would be making something else too. Probably wouldn't be nobody carrying a melody.
Well, the trumpet is resting while you're doing it, isn't he? Most of the time. And the clarinet would be running up in the air, up and down?

Up and down. Then sometimes work with the, you've got a good banjo player, bass player, piano, like that. You see? But neither your trombone nor the clarinet. At least the trumpet, they declared it. It would be in, after you, on your trombone, could be perfect on that, but you're going to do. See? Then your banjo and bass violin and piano would be going along with you. And then when they come in, it would be something different, all like that.
